region: Volta Grande of the Rio Xingu, Pará, Brazil
description: Endemic to the rocky rapids of the Rio Xingu's Volta Grande, where it hides in crevices between boulders; the male guards the large eggs and wrigglers inside his cave. Brazil banned its export in 2004, so the hobby now relies largely on captive-bred fish.

A Rio Xingu Hypancistrus whose cream-and-black tiger markings break into wavy lines that differ in every fish. One of the easier Hypancistrus to spawn: the male fans the egg clump in a narrow cave until the fry leave.
A Rio Xingu Hypancistrus with bold yellow-to-white worm-like lines on black that vary from fish to fish. It is prolific in captivity, and breeding males defend their cave vigorously.
A rare and costly Xingu Hypancistrus whose white body is broken by irregular black blotches unique to each fish. Its relationship to the zebra and king tiger plecos is still unresolved.
A small Hypancistrus from the lower Rio Tapajós covered in a fine white maze ('arabesque') on black. Males guard eggs in caves and spawn readily in warm, soft, well-oxygenated water.

region: Rio Casiquiare & upper Rio Negro, Venezuela & Brazil
description: Described from the Casiquiare canal that links the Orinoco and Rio Negro, it is dark grey to black with large white spots. It grows larger than most Hypancistrus and males are quarrelsome over caves.
An Orinoco Hypancistrus sprinkled with small white spots and trimmed with white on the dorsal and caudal fins. Spot size varies between collecting sites, giving several trade forms.

Exported from the Colombian Orinoco drainage as the 'Colombian zebra', this small Hypancistrus was named H. debilittera in 2007. Its pale, broken bands on dark brown are far less regular than the true zebra's.
A small, rarely exported Hypancistrus from the Rio Xingu, dark with fine pale dots. Like its relatives it is a cave-spawning male brooder that prefers meaty foods to algae.
A blackwater bristlenose that is jet black with tiny white dots and white seams on the dorsal and caudal fins, boldest in young fish. Males grow branched snout tentacles and guard eggs in caves.

A jet-black bristlenose from fast, rocky stretches of the Xingu and Tocantins. Unlike other Ancistrus, both sexes wear a dense 'medusa' mane of branched tentacles around the snout, and it needs strong current and plenty of oxygen.

A widespread bristlenose whose dark body carries fewer, larger pale spots than the common bristlenose. Populations differ in spot size, and several imported forms with their own L-numbers belong to this species.

A xanthic, lemon-yellow Ancistrus first collected in Paraguay; the captive strain sold as L144a has dark blue eyes, which separates it from red-eyed albino bristlenose. Males grow snout bristles and guard eggs in caves.
A long-established albino strain of the common bristlenose: pinkish-yellow with faint pale spots and red eyes. It behaves and breeds exactly like the wild form, the male guarding the eggs in a cave.
A captive-bred bristlenose line with greatly elongated, flowing fins. The long fins tear more easily, so it is best kept away from fin-nipping tankmates.
Combines the albino and long-fin bristlenose traits: a pale yellow-pink fish with red eyes and veil-like fins. Like other bristlenose it rasps algae and biofilm and spawns in caves.
A line-bred bristlenose selected for an intense orange-red body and fins. Colour is strongest in well-fed adults; care and breeding match the wild form.
A captive-bred bristlenose with an orange-to-yellow body blotched irregularly with black, so no two fish look alike. Biology and care match the wild-type bristlenose.
A small, sturdy pleco with dark brown saddles over a tan-yellow body. It grazes biofilm and soft wood and spawns in caves, the male guarding the eggs.

Known for years only as L134, the Leopard Frog Pleco was formally described in 2010 from the Rio Tapajós; its black bands on bright yellow are boldest in juveniles. It stays small and breeds readily in caves.
Larger and more boldly spotted than most Peckoltia, it is a widespread species sold under several L-numbers (L075, L124, L301). It rasps wood and biofilm and readily takes meaty foods.

region: Orinoco & Amazon basins, Venezuela, Colombia & Brazil
description: One of the few fishes that feeds on wood itself: it gouges driftwood with spoon-shaped teeth, and the shavings make up much of its diet. Wild fish show thin black lines on grey and often red eyes, and adults are intolerant of other large plecos.

region: Rio Tocantins, Araguaia, Xingu & Tapajós basins, Brazil
description: A large wood-eating Panaque from the clear-water rivers of the Brazilian Shield, sold under the L027 group with names such as 'thunder' and 'platinum' royal. Juveniles show fine dark lines that fade toward a plain grey-gold in adults, which grow long caudal filaments.

The blue-eyed panaque of Colombia's Magdalena and Cauca rivers: a plain grey-black wood eater with striking turquoise-blue eyes. It tolerates cooler water than the Amazonian Panaque but still needs driftwood to rasp.
A small loricariid whose dark body is crossed by irregular orange-tan bands; it rasps soft driftwood, which forms a real part of its diet. Males guard the eggs in tight caves.
The 'flash pleco' of Peru's upper Amazon, black with bright white worm-like lines; it was described in 2013, the name meaning 'white worm'. Like all Panaqolus it needs driftwood to rasp.
A tiger-banded Panaqolus from the Rio Tocantins, tan with numerous dark brown bars, and one of the very first fishes to receive an L-number. It rasps wood and spawns in caves.

The Gold Nugget Pleco grazes aufwuchs on sunlit rocks in the Rio Xingu; its black body carries golden spots, and the dorsal and caudal fins have broad yellow seams. L018 is the large-spotted form, and adults become quarrelsome with other plecos.
A small-spotted population of the Gold Nugget Pleco traded as L081. It is the same species as L018 and needs the same warm, fast, oxygen-rich water and algae-rich diet.
The Rio Iriri population of the Gold Nugget Pleco, with finer spots than L018 and L081. Like the other forms it grazes aufwuchs and turns territorial toward other plecos as it matures.

A large, heavy-bodied Baryancistrus from clear-water tributaries of the lower Amazon, black with sharp white spots; it is sold under L026 and L142. It grazes algae and grows too big for most home aquaria.

The low-finned 'L200': an olive-green Baryancistrus densely dotted with lime-yellow, from the clear, fast Río Ventuari and upper Orinoco. It needs strong current, high oxygen and a vegetable-rich diet.

Sold as the 'blue panaque', this Baryancistrus is a nearly uniform blue-grey with an orange seam along the dorsal fin. It was described in 2009 from the upper Orinoco, where it grazes aufwuchs on rocks in fast water.

The high-finned 'L200': a lime-spotted green pleco with a taller dorsal fin than the look-alike Baryancistrus demantoides, with which it shares the Río Ventuari. It needs fast, warm, oxygen-rich water and plenty of vegetable food.

The 'blue phantom' is a slate-blue loricariid peppered with small pale spots, exported from the Venezuelan Orinoco; spot size varies between imports. It eats both meaty foods and vegetable matter and defends its patch from rivals.

The Sunshine Pleco of the Rio Xingu is black with golden spots and wide yellow-orange fin margins. Its few, large spoon-shaped teeth are adapted for cracking snails and other invertebrates, and adults are territorial.

The Tapajós counterpart of the sunshine pleco, with smaller and denser golden spots than S. aureatus; it is also traded as L133. A large snail-eating loricariid that needs a big, warm, fast-flowing tank.
Formerly placed in Oligancistrus, this loricariid is black and densely peppered with tiny white spots. It lives in rock crevices in strong current and feeds on biofilm, algae and small invertebrates.

A broad, flat loricariid of rocky Xingu and Tocantins rapids, known for switching between slate-grey and patchy or complete orange-yellow colouring. It grazes algae and biofilm with a wide sucker mouth and needs strong current.

region: Rio Negro & upper Orinoco, Brazil & Venezuela
description: One of the flat-bodied blackwater 'butterfly plecos', banded in brown and cream, its depressed body letting it cling to wood and rock in current. Breeding males develop bristly odontodes along the head and pectoral spines.

region: Rio Tocantins & lower Amazon tributaries, Brazil
description: The 'vampire pleco': a black loricariid sprinkled with white stars, whose long, tusk-like premaxillary teeth pick snails and other invertebrates from crevices. Males become territorial around caves and can be rough with other bottom dwellers.
The Sultan Pleco of the Rio Tapajós is pale grey with bold black spots and a tall, spotted dorsal fin. It stays smaller than other Leporacanthicus and feeds on snails and meaty foods.

Named for the three orange 'beacons' at the tips of its dorsal fin and both caudal lobes, this Orinoco Leporacanthicus uses its long teeth to extract snails. It has been bred in aquaria, the male guarding eggs in a deep cave.

region: Rio Branco & Essequibo basins, Brazil & Guyana
description: The Leopard Cactus Pleco is covered in rough, spiny plates and bold black spots on tan, with red-orange fin margins. A meat-eating, highly territorial loricariid that needs its own cave and plenty of space.

A large, spiny charcoal-grey loricariid with blood-red fins; its species name borrows 'pirarara', the Brazilian name of the redtail catfish. It eats meaty foods and is notoriously aggressive toward other plecos.

A giant spiny loricariid with a lyre-shaped tail whose filaments trail behind it; juveniles are black with white polka dots that fade as they grow. It can approach a metre in the wild and suits only very large aquaria.
A uniformly black, heavily spined loricariid with long caudal filaments, widespread in the Amazon. Hardy and omnivorous, but it grows too large and too territorial for most home tanks.

The most widespread 'common pleco': an Amazonian sailfin with leopard-spotted brown armour that grows past 35 cm. It digs nesting burrows in riverbanks, and released fish have become invasive in warm waters worldwide.
A farm-bred albino form of the sailfin pleco, pale yellow with faint spotting and red eyes. Its biology matches the wild type, including the large adult size.

A large sailfin pleco with a tall dorsal fin and a raised bony ridge on the nape; its tan body is covered in a dark brown honeycomb of spots. A heavy-bodied grazer of algae and detritus for very large tanks.

A sailfin pleco from the Tocantins and Araguaia, dark with sharp golden spots on body and fins; it is traded as L001 and L022. It stays smaller than most Pterygoplichthys but still needs a large tank and plenty of vegetable food.
A large brown sailfin pleco with dark spots and a long, many-rayed dorsal fin. It can gulp air to survive oxygen-poor water and has established invasive populations outside South America.

A dark brown sailfin pleco covered in pale yellow worm-like lines rather than spots. Native to the Madeira basin, it is one of the main invasive 'armoured catfish' in Florida, Mexico and Southeast Asia.

region: Paraná & Paraguay basins, Argentina, Brazil & Paraguay
description: A sailfin pleco of the Paraná and Paraguay rivers, dark brown to black with creamy spots. Being subtropical, it tolerates cooler water than its Amazonian relatives and is a powerful algae grazer.
A chocolate-brown sailfin pleco with rough, prickly armour that gives it a rugged look. A peaceful grazer of algae and detritus from the upper Amazon.

region: Coastal rivers of the Guianas, northeastern South America
description: The species that gave plecos their name, from coastal rivers of the Guianas; its tall dorsal fin has far fewer rays than a sailfin pleco's. Many fish sold as 'Hypostomus plecostomus' are actually Pterygoplichthys.
A golden-yellow Hypostomus from the subtropical Rio Uruguay, prized for its unusual colour and happiest in cooler water than most plecos. A large grazer of algae and biofilm.

region: Rio Negro & Orinoco basins, Brazil & Venezuela
description: A flattened blackwater pleco with dark saddles over a grey-brown body, larger than its cousin D. pulchra. Mature males grow long odontodes on the head and along the flanks.

The Rubber-lip or 'bulldog' pleco comes from cool, fast Andean streams and needs well-oxygenated, current-swept water rather than tropical warmth. It scrapes algae from rocks with a broad, fleshy mouth.
A brown, spotted loricariid recognised by the whisker-like odontodes on its cheeks, found across the Amazon and Orinoco. A hardy grazer of algae and biofilm for medium-sized tanks.

region: Paraguay & Paraná basins, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil & Paraguay
description: A slender, flattened loricariid that rests motionless on sand, camouflaged by mottled tan saddles. Breeding males grow bristles along the sides of the head and guard the eggs inside a tube or cave.

region: Amazon & Paraguay basins, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay & Peru
description: A reddish-brown whiptail with dark saddles and a long whip-like upper caudal ray. Like other Rineloricaria, the male cleans a tube or cave and fans the eggs until they hatch.
A rust-red whiptail known only by its trade code L010a and now kept mainly as a captive-bred strain. It breeds readily, the male guarding the eggs in a tube.

Mimics a submerged stick with its long rostrum and pencil-thin body, grazing algae among plants and wood in slow Orinoco waters. The male guards eggs laid on glass or wood; many fish sold as F. acus are in fact this species.
A slender, high-finned loricariid (formerly Sturisoma panamense) with long filaments on both caudal lobes. Males grow a beard of cheek odontodes and guard eggs laid in rows on glass or wood.

The largest commonly kept Sturisoma-type catfish (formerly Sturisoma aureum), golden-brown with a sail-like dorsal fin and long caudal filaments. It comes from Colombia's Magdalena drainage and needs clean, current-swept water.

A delicate Sturisoma-like loricariid with very long filaments on the first rays of its dorsal, pectoral and caudal fins. It grazes algae in flowing upper-Amazon rivers and is sensitive to poor water quality.
A sand-coloured, very flat whiptail that sifts soft sand for small invertebrates in Amazon and Orinoco rivers. The male carries the egg mass attached to his enlarged lower lip until the fry hatch.

A broad, flat, sand-coloured loricariid that buries itself in sand with only its eyes showing, sifting for small invertebrates. As in Loricaria, the male broods the eggs attached beneath his lower lip.
Has a long, pointed rostrum ending in a soft tip, used to probe sand for tiny invertebrates. The male carries the eggs on his lower lip, a habit shared with Loricaria.

Spends much of its time swimming belly-up beneath leaves and driftwood, and its reversed countershading—a dark belly under a paler back—camouflages it in that position. It lives in groups and has spawned in aquarium caves.

A Lake Tanganyika squeaker, pale with crisp black spots and white-edged black fins, that hunts invertebrates among rocks at dusk. Many fish sold under this name are really S. lucipinnis or hybrids; true S. petricola is larger and has bigger spots.
Described in 2006, it is smaller than S. petricola, with finer spots and brilliant white fin margins (the name means 'light fins'). It is the Tanganyikan squeaker most often bred commercially.

A brood parasite: groups slip their eggs among those of spawning mouthbrooding cichlids, and the catfish fry hatch first and eat the cichlid eggs in the mother's mouth. Large-eyed and boldly spotted (often sold as 'S. multipunctatus').

region: Nile, Niger, Chad & Volta basins, West & Central Africa
description: Named for the long, feathery filaments trailing from its tall dorsal fin. A hardy African catfish that sometimes feeds upside-down at the surface and squeaks by grinding its pectoral spines when handled.
A deep violet-black squeaker with white spots and white-banded fins, long prized for its contrast (often sold as 'S. angelicus'). It is shy and nocturnal and needs caves and subdued light.

Has bold dark spots on beige, black-striped tail lobes and a long filament trailing from its dorsal fin. A placid, nocturnal Congo species (often sold as 'S. decorus') that grows large and lives for decades.

region: Central Congo basin (Cuvette Centrale), DR Congo
description: One of the most colourful Synodontis, with dark brown stripes running the length of a yellow-orange body (often sold as 'S. flavitaeniatus'). It comes from slow, forested rivers of the central Congo basin and is relatively peaceful.
Has unusually large eyes and maxillary barbels that can stretch longer than its body. Peaceful for a Synodontis, it forages over soft bottoms at dusk.

region: Lower Congo rapids, DR Congo & Republic of the Congo
description: A rapids specialist from the lower Congo with a flattened body, dark brown with narrow pale vertical bands. It needs strong current and high oxygen, grazing and foraging among rocks.

A dark, rough-skinned squeaker of Lake Tanganyika's rocky shores, near-black with white-edged fins (often sold as 'S. granulosus'). It rasps aufwuchs and hunts invertebrates among rocks and is territorial toward other catfish.

region: Senegal, Gambia, Niger, Volta & Chad basins, West Africa
description: A large West African squeaker whose grey flanks carry dark, pale-ringed eyespots (ocelli), the source of its name. Hardy and long-lived, it eventually needs a large tank.
A cream-to-yellow squeaker covered in a maze of brown lines that differs on every fish. A relatively peaceful, nocturnal Congo species that prefers soft, slightly acidic water.
The only Synodontis endemic to Lake Malawi, beige with dark spots, foraging over sand and rock at night. Its hard, alkaline water needs make it a natural catfish for Malawi cichlid tanks.

region: Pool Malebo region of the Congo, DR Congo & Republic of the Congo
description: A small Congo squeaker with a broad, blunt snout that, like S. nigriventris, often swims belly-up and has a darker belly than back. Peaceful and happiest in a small group.

A plain silvery-grey squeaker with one, sometimes two, large black spots on each flank—the count can differ between the two sides (often sold as 'S. notatus'). A sturdy Congo species that becomes territorial with age.

region: West & Central Africa (Senegal & Gambia to the Nile)
description: Often swims inverted like S. nigriventris and likewise has a darker belly than back, but grows considerably larger. Widespread across the Sahelian rivers of West and Central Africa.

region: Nile & West African basins (Niger, Chad, Volta, Senegal)
description: A plain grey, large Synodontis common across North and West African rivers, where it is also fished for food. Adults are robust and quarrelsome and need a big tank with sturdy tankmates.

region: Nile, Niger, Chad, Volta & Senegal basins
description: Its maxillary barbels are joined by a broad membrane, used to sieve zooplankton while it swims upside-down in open water. A large, gentle West African squeaker with a darker belly than back.

region: Nile, Niger, Chad, Volta, Senegal & Gambia basins
description: A grey squeaker with a striking orange-red caudal fin, widespread from the Nile to Senegal. Juveniles are spotted and adults plain; it grows large and is very hardy.

region: Nile, Niger, Chad, Senegal & Volta basins
description: Formerly Brachysynodontis, it spends much of its life swimming belly-up and feeding at the surface, with the dark belly and pale back that suit that posture. A deep-bodied, peaceful West African squeaker.
A tiny, secretive relative of Synodontis from Central African forest streams, banded in dark brown and tan. It hides in crevices by day and hunts small invertebrates at night.
A small, mottled-brown mochokid from the forest streams of Sierra Leone and Guinea and the only member of its genus. Shy and nocturnal, it suits a quiet community tank with caves.

A heavily armoured thorny catfish with a white stripe running from snout to tail on a black body; it croaks using its pectoral spines and swim bladder. Most fish traded as P. costatus are this species.
The white-spotted talking catfish: black with white spots and a white-banded tail, armoured with serrated lateral scutes. It hides by day, often wedged into crevices, and forages in the dark.
A mottled brown thorny catfish with a pale stripe along its scutes that buries itself in sand or leaf litter by day. It produces audible croaks with its pectoral spines and swim bladder.

region: Lower Amazon & coastal rivers of the Guianas
description: A small, heavily spined doradid mottled in chocolate and cream, living in coastal rivers and even brackish estuaries. It burrows by day and "talks" with grating pectoral spines.
A spiny, mottled brown doradid with a pale band along its thorny lateral scutes. It grunts audibly using its pectoral spines and swim bladder and spends the day buried or wedged in wood.

region: Amazon basin (incl. Rio Negro), Brazil & Peru
description: One of the smallest doradids at about 3.5 cm, a stout little thorny catfish with pale saddles on dark brown. It hides in leaf litter and wood by day and needs very peaceful company.
An Orinoco thorny catfish with a more elongate body and pointed snout than most doradids, greyish-brown with darker mottling. It sifts sand and detritus for invertebrates at night.

A huge thorny catfish with tall, hooked lateral scutes, known in the trade as the 'mother of snails' for its mollusc-crushing diet. It exceeds half a metre and is a gentle giant for public aquaria and very large tanks.
One of the largest doradids, named for the saw-like row of scutes along its flanks. It sucks up mud and sand to sift out invertebrates and detritus—a gentle but enormous fish for public aquaria.
A large, peaceful doradid that feeds on fruit, seeds and molluscs and migrates with seasonal floods. Its rough, spotted skin and thorny scutes make it a durable display fish for big aquaria.
A small woodcat, dark brown with scattered cream spots, that spends the day wedged into crevices in driftwood. Like all auchenipterids it fertilises internally, the male using a modified anal fin.

region: Rio Negro & middle Amazon, Brazil, Peru & Venezuela
description: Cream-yellow overlaid with a bold network of dark brown blotches, a pattern that varies by locality. A nocturnal woodcat of blackwater rivers that will swallow small fish.

region: Tropical South America (Amazon, Orinoco, Paraná & Guianas)
description: A mottled brown, big-mouthed woodcat that rests in hollow logs by day and hunts insects and small fish at night. Like its relatives it fertilises internally, the male using a modified anal fin.
A big-headed catfish banded in dark brown and yellow, with a cavernous mouth for engulfing fish at night. It spends the day motionless in a cave or under wood.

region: Venezuela & Colombia (Orinoco tributaries & Lake Valencia basin)
description: A small, chunky catfish banded in black-brown and yellow. It hides in caves by day and will eat fry or very small fish at night.

region: Orinoco & upper Rio Negro basins, Venezuela
description: A naked catfish that mimics Corydoras, copying their eye bar and dark dorsal blotch so it can shoal with them unnoticed. It forages over sand alongside its armoured models.
A slender, silvery catfish with a dark stripe along the flank and very long maxillary barbels. It forages actively in loose groups at night, and its pectoral spines carry a painful venom.

region: Amazon & Orinoco basins, Colombia, Peru & Venezuela
description: A restless, silver, black-spotted pimelodid whose barbels reach past its tail fin, active mainly at night in groups. Its sharp, venomous fin spines snag in nets, and it will eat neon-sized tankmates.

region: Amazon, Orinoco, Paraná basins & the Guianas
description: Silvery with a broad dark band along the upper flank and a black blotch on the dorsal fin. Larger than the pictus, it roams open water at dusk and will eat any fish it can swallow.
Dark grey above with a white belly band and a brick-red tail. Sold as small juveniles, it reaches a metre or more, swallows anything that fits, and outgrows almost every home aquarium.
A big pimelodid with a tall, sail-like dorsal fin and bold dark marbling on tan. A nocturnal predator suited to public aquaria or giant tanks.
Has a flattened, spoon-shaped snout and a black stripe running from snout to the lower tail lobe. It rests among roots and plants by day and hunts small fish at night.
A long, flat-headed predator with dark vertical bars and spots over grey above a white belly. A prized food and sport fish that grows far too large for home aquaria.
Resembles the barred sorubim, but its dark bands form loops and wavy lines rather than straight bars. A powerful nocturnal predator for public aquaria and very large tanks.
Cream to golden with bold black bands and extremely long barbels. A fast-swimming Amazonian predator that needs open swimming space in a very large aquarium.
Endemic to the Lake Maracaibo basin, it is pale with a bold network of dark blotches and long barbels. A nocturnal predator kept mainly by large-catfish specialists.
Has a flat, projecting lower jaw and a row of large round dark spots along each flank. A placid but piscivorous pimelodid that rests on the bottom by day and hunts at night.

The 'piracatinga' is a grey, dark-spotted pimelodid with sharp teeth that scavenges carcasses and bites chunks from live fish. Its fishery, which used river dolphins and caimans as bait, was suspended in Brazil.

Almost perfectly transparent, with its skeleton visible and its organs packed into a small silvery sac behind the head; long sold as K. bicirrhis or K. minor until described in 2013. It hovers in mid-water shoals and pines away if kept alone.

region: South & Southeast Asia (India to Indochina & Java)
description: A silvery, compressed silurid with a dark shoulder spot that swims in mid-water with a long, rippling anal fin. Valued as a food fish in South Asia, it eats small fish in aquaria.

region: Central & Eastern Europe to western Asia
description: Europe's largest freshwater fish: a scaleless giant with a broad head, six barbels and a long anal fin running to the tail. Shown in public aquaria and large ponds, it is a nocturnal ambush predator that can exceed 2.5 m in the wild.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
description: A skittish, shoaling catfish farmed in huge numbers in Vietnam as 'tra' or 'swai'. Sold as shimmering striped juveniles, it grows past a metre, panics and crashes into glass, and outgrows home aquaria.
A farm-produced albino form of the iridescent shark, pinkish-white with red eyes. It shares the wild type's huge adult size and nervous, shoaling nature.

One of the largest freshwater fishes, reaching about 3 m; adults are toothless, barbel-less grazers of algae and plants. Critically endangered in the wild, it is displayed in public aquaria and stocked from hatcheries.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
description: A fast, predatory pangasiid with a long trailing filament on its dorsal and pectoral fins. It reaches around 3 m, is critically endangered in the wild, and belongs only in public aquaria.

region: Pacific coast of the Americas, Mexico to Peru
description: A silvery sea catfish with black, white-edged fins, sold as a freshwater fish although adults need brackish to marine water. In the wild the male broods the large eggs in his mouth; in aquaria it shoals actively and eats small fish.

Juveniles form dense, rolling 'balls' over sand and reef, then become solitary as they grow. Its fin spines are highly venomous, and the second dorsal and anal fins merge with the tail into one eel-like fin.

region: India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan
description: The 'pyjama catfish', a slender bagrid of South Asian rivers and ponds with dark and pale stripes along the flanks and long barbels. Active at dusk in loose groups, it may eat very small tankmates.

region: Ganges–Brahmaputra & Indus basins (India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: Very like M. vittatus, with dark longitudinal stripes and a distinct dark shoulder spot; the two are often traded interchangeably as 'striped' or 'pyjama' catfish. Peaceful toward fish too large to swallow.
A slate-black bagrid from Myanmar that habitually swims and rests belly-up beneath overhangs. It grows fairly large and will eat small fish.
Formerly Leiocassis siamensis, it has broad chocolate bands on yellow-tan and hides in caves by day. It becomes territorial with age and eats small fish at night.

region: Mekong & Chao Phraya basins, Southeast Asia
description: A big, grey bagrid from the Mekong with a bright red tail fin and long barbels. It is an aggressive, fast-growing predator that eventually needs a tank of thousands of litres.
A velvet-black bagrid with an arched back and an extremely tall, spiny dorsal fin, from rivers of Sundaland. Nocturnal and shy, it sifts the bottom for insect larvae and needs soft, acidic water.
A small, chunky catfish of rocky shores that hides in caves, where pairs guard their eggs and fry. When stressed its skin secretes a toxic mucus that can kill tankmates in a confined space.

region: West & Central Africa (Nile, Niger, Chad & Congo basins)
description: Tan with a giraffe-like network of brown patches and a long pointed snout used to dig through sand for food. Peaceful but large, it uproots plants and needs a big tank as it grows.

A tiny stream catfish with granular skin, brown with pale yellowish saddles, that hides among stones and leaf litter by day. Its small size and secretive habits suit a species tank with cool, flowing water.

region: Ganges, Brahmaputra & Indus basins (India, Bangladesh, Nepal & Pakistan)
description: A small, cream catfish with dark brown saddles and banded tail lobes, from sandy, flowing rivers of northern South Asia. It shoals over sand and prefers cooler, well-oxygenated water.

region: Rocky rivers of South & Southeast Asia (Indus to Mekong)
description: A huge sisorid of fast, rocky rivers with a flattened head, mottled saddles and a sharply forked tail. Occasionally shown in public aquaria, it can exceed 2 m and is notorious in Himalayan rivers for its size.
A 3 cm erethistid with broad, spiny pectoral fins it uses to wedge itself in place in flowing water. Mottled brown, it sits motionless on leaves and stones and needs very small live foods.

Has a broad, flat head and a slender tail like a banjo's neck, with warty brown skin that makes it look like a dead leaf. It buries itself in sand by day and can jet forward by forcing water out of its gill openings.

region: Coastal rivers & estuaries of the Guianas and the Amazon delta
description: A very flat-headed banjo catfish with a long, tapering tail, living in coastal rivers and estuaries. The female carries her eggs stuck to spongy stalks (cotylephores) on her belly until they hatch.

region: Congo basin (DR Congo, Republic of the Congo & Gabon)
description: A semi-transparent, silvery catfish with three black stripes along each side running into the tail lobes. Unlike most catfish it swims actively in mid-water by day and must be kept in a group.

region: Indus, Ganges & Brahmaputra basins (Pakistan, India, Nepal & Bangladesh)
description: A translucent, silvery schooling catfish that has no dorsal fin at all but keeps a small adipose fin, swimming in open water with a long rippling anal fin. It needs cool, flowing, well-oxygenated water and a group of its own kind.

Breathes air through a branched organ above its gills and can wriggle across land between ponds using its pectoral spines. Invasive in Florida and banned in several US states, it is a voracious predator that escapes from uncovered tanks.
Pinkish-white with red eyes, the albino is more often sold than the wild-coloured form. It shares the species' air-breathing, land-crossing habits and predatory appetite.

An eel-like clariid with no pectoral or pelvic fins ('apus' means footless), living in swamps of the Congo basin. It burrows in soft mud and leaf litter and breathes air when the water is short of oxygen.
Lies motionless among leaf litter, camouflaged by warty brown skin, and wiggles its tiny barbels as lures. When a fish comes close it opens its enormous mouth and engulfs surprisingly large prey.

A reddish-brown, warty frogmouth catfish of Sundaland peat swamps, with a huge flat head and a gape that swallows passing fish. It sits so still among leaves that it is easily overlooked, moving only to strike.

region: West & Central Africa and the Nile basin
description: Can discharge several hundred volts from an electric organ wrapped around its body, stunning prey and deterring attackers. It has no rayed dorsal fin, only an adipose fin, and must be kept alone.

region: South Asia & Myanmar (Pakistan to Myanmar, Sri Lanka)
description: Paired air sacs run back from its gills, letting it survive in stagnant, oxygen-poor ponds. Its pectoral spines carry a potent venom, and stings are a familiar hazard to South Asian fishers.
North America's most-farmed fish: a fork-tailed, blue-grey catfish scattered with small black spots that fade in large adults. A common public-aquarium and pond fish that eats almost anything.
Produced on fish farms and sold as pond and aquarium fish, albino channel catfish are creamy white with pink-red eyes. They share the wild form's hardiness and large adult size.
A hardy, mottled olive-brown catfish with a square tail, tolerant of cold and oxygen-poor water. Both parents guard the eggs and then shepherd the dense black ball of fry.
A small, plain yellowish-brown catfish whose adipose fin merges with its rounded tail. It hides in vegetation and debris by day, and its pectoral spines carry a mild venom.

A rounded tail, yellowish belly and white chin barbels set it apart from the dark-barbelled brown and black bullheads. Hardy and tolerant of cool water, it nests under logs or banks, where the parents guard the young.

region: Mississippi & Gulf Coast drainages, North America
description: A broad, flattened head with a projecting lower jaw and mottled olive-brown skin mark this big ictalurid. Unlike the channel catfish it takes almost only live prey, ambushing fish from cover at night, and grows well over a metre.

region: Mississippi, Ohio & Missouri basins and Gulf drainages, North America
description: North America's largest catfish: a slate-blue, fork-tailed ictalurid without the channel catfish's black spots and with a long, straight-edged anal fin. It is a centrepiece of big-river exhibits in public aquaria.

region: Murray–Darling basin & eastern coastal rivers, Australia
description: Eastern Australia's eel-tailed catfish, whose second dorsal, caudal and anal fins merge into one tail fin. In spring the male builds a circular nest of gravel and guards the eggs; it is kept by native-fish enthusiasts and in public aquaria.
